stories.title: Why Malaysia's internet exchange build-out is moving to the Thai border
stories.summary: Open DC is developing an internet exchange at Bukit Kayu Hitam in Kedah, near the Thai border, designed to keep Malaysian and regional traffic from routing through Singapore. Four submarine cable landing stations, two Malaysian and two Thai, lie within reach of the site.
stories.why_it_matters: Keeping traffic domestic strengthens Malaysia's internet sovereignty and reduces latency and cost dependence on Singapore's hubs. It also reframes border-region data centres as energy-export infrastructure, leveraging Malaysia's power advantages.
stories.content:
- **Open DC is betting that a Malaysia internet exchange at the Kedah border can keep regional traffic out of Singapore.**
- **The operator frames data centres as an energy-export business and is pushing cooling-knowledge transfer to local vendors.**

Four cable landing stations sit within reach of Bukit Kayu Hitam in Kedah: two in Malaysia and two across the border in Thailand, at Satun and Songkhla, roughly 50 to 60 kilometres apart on opposite coasts. Traffic arriving at those stations today largely travels to Bangkok, or down to Kuala Lumpur and Singapore, before it can be exchanged.

Open DC is building an internet exchange at that border on the argument that it should not have to. The company launched D8-1 in the Delapan Special Border Economic Zone after being invited four years ago to replicate, at the northern frontier, the model it had already built in Johor Bahru. The site takes its name from Delapan, the Malay word for eight, because the company wanted something tied to the place, managing director Wong Weng Yew said at a media briefing in Kuala Lumpur on Monday.

The Johor exchange helped pull Singapore players across the Causeway, Wong said, and the northern project is the same play aimed at Thai and Chinese traffic. Johor also had Singapore’s moratorium and land constraints pushing demand north, which the Kedah project has no equivalent of.

The company’s parent, Extreme Broadband, is a licensed Malaysian telco that has been selling enterprise connectivity since 2005. That history explains a pitch built on carriers and peering while most of the market talks in megawatts.

### What a Malaysia internet exchange changes

An internet exchange is a shared point where networks hand traffic to each other directly instead of paying a third party to carry it. Open DC already runs or hosts them at its other sites, including JBIX in Johor and a transport node for DE-CIX Malaysia’s Penang Internet Exchange at PE2, which makes D8-1 a repeat of a model the company has built before rather than a first attempt.

Wong described the model in terms of air travel. “What we are doing essentially is like building an airport,” he said, adding that airlines bring passenger traffic into a hub where passengers change flights, and networks do the same with traffic at an exchange.

The savings come off the transit bill. Leasing a 10G link from Delapan down to Singapore would cost in the region ofRM100,000 a year, Wong said, describing the figure as indicative. Traffic exchanged locally at a northern exchange avoids that line item, and the cost falls further as more networks join and more traffic stays in the north.

Wong’s case is that traffic landing at Satun or Songkhla and destined for elsewhere in the region has no technical reason to detour through a hub several hundred kilometres away, which adds both cost and latency.

The count of carriers inside a facility is what makes that possible, and it is where Open DC’s numbers are unusual. Two carriers are considered good for most enterprise sites, Wong said, while Open DC’s data centres typically carry at least six and JB1 in Johor has more than 15. Tenants can buy connectivity from Chinese, Singaporean, European, Indian and US telcos without leaving the building, a mix he said is almost impossible for other operators to replicate.

The exchange at D8-1 is not fully live. Wong said a capacity upgrade prompted by demand pushed the rollout back by several months, with a full launch targeted for the end of this year or January. He declined to name the networks waiting to connect, citing non-disclosure agreements. The project was conceived four years ago, which makes the launch a fair measure of how quickly regional traffic shifts once a new exchange opens.

### Complementing rather than competing

Thailand has drawn substantial hyperscale investment, and Open DC’s Kedah capacity, at 2MW expanding to 4MW, is not in that contest. Wong said the aim is a connectivity hub serving the wider region rather than a play for the Thai market, and that Thai networks connecting at the border would reduce what they send to Singapore and pay less to do it.

He made the same argument about Singapore. Cable density concentrated in one small area creates a chokepoint, and northern Malaysian capacity gives networks somewhere to park a second copy of their traffic. “If something happens to the south, the north will carry on,” he said.

Open DC’s own portfolio runs from JB1 and JB2 in Johor through CJ1 in Cyberjaya to PE1 and PE2 in Penang and D8-1 at the border, a north-to-south corridor Wong said no other operator is developing. More than 90% of its business comes from overseas customers, he said, with a recent surge in East Asian traffic, drawn from a base the company puts at over 300 organisations, including Fortune 500 names.

### Compute as an export

Wong put a different frame on what his industry sells, describing it as “an energy export business”. A data centre takes power generated in Malaysia, converts it into compute capacity, and sells that capacity to foreign customers who pay in US dollars.

He does not expect the industry to keep growing on fossil generation, and said siting capacity in the north lets Open DC tap renewable options there. He put rough numbers on what that would involve, saying that supplying 15% of PE2’s electricity from solar would mean signing a contract with a solar provider worth around RM150 million. He stressed that the company is still debating the level and has not committed.

Solar developers need long tenures to build, and Wong said few buyers are willing to sign a 10-year commitment. He named battery energy storage as a second area where data centre demand pulls research and development into the country.

### Building vendors rather than importing them

On talent, Open DC’s approach runs through its supply chain. Wong said the company selects local vendors and places them alongside global equipment suppliers, then requires those suppliers to transfer knowledge and train the local firms as part of supplying Open DC.

Precision cooling is the example he gave. AI workloads impose demanding cooling requirements, and the systems involved are ones local vendors rarely get to work on unless a customer creates the opening. “Hopefully we can sow a seed in the local market that we can grow into a tree of talents in the local communities,” Wong said.

The financing history suggests why he emphasises local capability. Wong said Malaysian banks were unfamiliar with data centres when Open DC started in 2015, and that one of its first funders was a Singaporean infrastructure fund. Alternative lenders moved before the banks did, and he said many local institutions remain hesitant today.

Whether the Malaysia internet exchange delivers depends on the networks Wong says are waiting.

stories.title: Computing power satellite launched from Jiuquan, China
stories.summary: Beijing Enterprise Satellite’s “Super Intelligent Computing 1” computing power satellite was successfully launched into orbit at 12:03 on September 20 aboard the Lijian 1 Yao 18 carrier rocket from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center. The satellite is designed to process and analyze data in orbit, reducing the need to send large volumes of satellite data […]
stories.content:
Beijing Enterprise Satellite’s “Super Intelligent Computing 1” computing power satellite was successfully launched into orbit at 12:03 on September 20 aboard the Lijian 1 Yao 18 carrier rocket from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center. The satellite is designed to process and analyze data in orbit, reducing the need to send large volumes of satellite data to ground-based data centers for processing.

According to a press release, the satellite is equipped with an on-board intelligent computing processing unit and uses laser communication technology to connect with other satellites and share computing resources. It can perform remote-sensing data processing, AI inference and real-time data analysis in orbit, allowing selected data to be processed before being transmitted to the ground.

Li Peiyang, Chief Technology Officer, Superintelligent Computing, said, “In the past, data collected by satellites needed to be transmitted back to ground data centers for processing, but they faced core pain points such as limited bandwidth for massive data transmission, high ground computing latency, and low data utilization. Now with computing power satellites, satellites have real-time computing, intelligent analysis and collaborative processing capabilities in the sky, thus breaking the lagging operation mode of the past ‘Tiangan Tiansuan’, realizing ‘Tiangan Tiansuan’, and effectively solving problems such as data response delays.”

The Super Intelligent Computing satellite can carry out remote-sensing big data processing, AI inference and real-time data analysis while in orbit. By processing data before transmission, the system is intended to reduce the volume of data sent to ground stations and shorten the time required to obtain usable results.

The technology is intended for applications including emergency disaster response, natural resource management, ecological monitoring and marine resource exploration. Super Intelligent Computing also said the technology could be applied to urban governance and ecological monitoring in Beijing.

The launch is the first step in Super Intelligent Computing’s planned expansion of its in-orbit computing resources. Super Intelligent Computing will steadily advance the large-scale layout of “Super Intelligent Computing Constellation”, continue to expand on-orbit computing power resources, optimize the layout of spatial nodes, create a world-wide collaborative comprehensive network and accessible three-dimensional intelligent computing network.

stories.title: Vocus plans 4,000km Brisbane-Darwin fibre route
stories.summary: Vocus has announced a 4,000-km ducted fibre route linking Brisbane, Townsville and Darwin, with service expected by 2030. The project is the second under the Australian Digital Infrastructure Platform and takes the initiative beyond the Sydney-Melbourne corridor, with route planning and design already underway.
stories.why_it_matters: A ducted, carrier-grade route to Darwin creates a new northern connectivity spine, reducing reliance on southern paths for traffic heading to Asia. It also positions Darwin as a more serious interconnection point as cable landings multiply in northern Australia.
stories.content:
Australian operator Vocus has announced plans for a 4,000-kilometre ducted fibre route connecting Brisbane, Townsville and Darwin, expanding its Australian Digital Infrastructure Platform (ADIP) beyond the Sydney-Melbourne corridor. The Brisbane-Darwin route is the second project under ADIP and is expected to be ready for service in 2030. Vocus has begun route planning, technical design and customer engagement, with the network designed to accommodate up to 3,456 fibre cores.

Vocus CEO Andrés Irlando said the expansion reflects the increasing infrastructure requirements associated with AI and data centre investment. “Australia is in a period of unprecedented investment in AI infrastructure, data centres, and international connectivity, requiring exponential investment in new terrestrial and subsea fibre networks,” he said.

Irlando said northern Australia was becoming increasingly important for AI, cloud and digital services, with Queensland and the Northern Territory emerging as data centre locations and gateways to Asia and the US.

### Northern extension

The new route will extend Vocus’s existing northern Australian network, which includes the Darwin-Jakarta-Singapore Cable and North-West Cable System. CTO Nikos Katinakis said the Brisbane-Darwin corridor would provide additional capacity, route diversity and resilience while extending the ducted intercapital design Vocus introduced with its Sydney-Melbourne project.

That Sydney-Melbourne project, announced in June as the first ADIP deployment, involves approximately AUD 500 million of investment and is scheduled for service in 2029. Vocus said it will support up to 6,912 fibre cores, or 3,456 fibre pairs, using ducted infrastructure that allows additional cables to be installed without further major civil works.

Vocus has subsequently appointed UGL as development partner for the Sydney-Melbourne project, with early works covering route surveys, design, engineering, stakeholder engagement and cost modelling. The company has described ADIP as a multi-year programme involving thousands of kilometres of new fibre routes, thousands of fibre pairs and hundreds of terabits of additional capacity.

### Global link

The Brisbane-Darwin announcement also comes as Vocus expands its role in northern Australia’s international connectivity. Environmental filings reported by W.Media in July identified Darwin, Townsville and Karumba as proposed Australian landing locations for Meta’s Project Waterworth subsea cable, with Vocus responsible for environmental survey work associated with the proposed route.

The planned Waterworth alignment includes approximately 5,360km within Australian waters and would create new international cable landing points at Townsville and Karumba if the project proceeds.

The relationship between the two developments is not spelt out by Vocus in the latest announcement, and the Brisbane-Darwin project is a separate terrestrial network. However, the overlap in geography is notable: the new terrestrial route will connect Brisbane, Townsville and Darwin, while the proposed Waterworth infrastructure would establish subsea connectivity at Townsville and Darwin.

Vocus has positioned ADIP as a response to projected growth in Australian data centre and AI infrastructure. The company says commissioned market research indicates Australian data centre capacity could triple by 2030, with AI workloads expected to account for most future long-haul fibre demand. It also says existing fibre corridors are approaching higher utilisation as connectivity requirements increase.

Vocus said the Brisbane-Darwin project is currently in its early works phase. The operator has not disclosed the expected capital cost of the project.

stories.title: Intel Malaysia expands advanced packaging as AI chips grow more complex
stories.summary: Intel is scaling up its Penang advanced packaging operations in Malaysia to handle the increasingly complex task of assembling multi-chiplet AI processors. The company says the expansion requires a larger pool of semiconductor and AI engineering talent in the country.
stories.why_it_matters: Advanced packaging has become a critical chokepoint in AI chip supply, and Malaysia is positioning itself as an indispensable node in that chain. The expansion strengthens Malaysia's role in the AI hardware ecosystem but also sets up a regional talent competition.
stories.content:
- **Intel Malaysia expands Penang advanced packaging for AI chips.**
- **Intel Malaysia needs more semiconductor and AI talent.**

Intel is expanding its advanced packaging capabilities in Malaysia as AI processors become larger and more complex, increasing the manufacturing demands involved in combining multiple chiplets into complete systems.

In an exclusive interview with *Tech Wire Asia*, Lee Wei Chern, Vice President, Intel Foundry; General Manager, Intel Assembly Test Manufacturing; and Managing Director, Intel Malaysia, said advanced packaging is becoming increasingly important as chipmakers move towards more complex system designs.

“Advanced packaging has become a critical differentiator in the AI era,” Lee said. “As AI systems scale, the challenge is no longer just about producing individual chiplets but integrating them into complete systems that deliver the bandwidth, power efficiency and reliability that customers expect.”

### Packaging more complex AI chips

As AI chip packages grow larger and combine chiplets made using different process technologies, assembly and test operations have to manage multiple manufacturing challenges within the same system.

Lee said Intel is working on technologies including EMIB-T, glass substrates and manufacturing processes designed to support larger form factors and higher performance.

“There is no single challenge when scaling to larger and more complex heterogeneous integration packages,” Lee said. “Thermal management, yield, interconnect and power delivery, and architecture co-design are all critical areas we focus on to ensure we deliver products with the right quality and reliability.”

Advanced packaging is also becoming an entry point for some customers working with Intel Foundry. Lee said customers are evaluating packaging technologies that allow chiplets made using different process technologies to be integrated into complete systems.

“Advanced packaging is increasingly becoming a strategic entry point for customers,” Lee said. “It creates opportunities to deepen relationships and support a broader range of foundry requirements as customers move toward more complex, system-level designs.”

Assembly Test Manufacturing remains part of that process, handling the manufacturing steps needed to deliver the final packaged product.

### Penang expands its manufacturing role

Intel’s new advanced packaging facility in Penang, scheduled to begin operations this year, will expand the company’s manufacturing capabilities in Malaysia.

Intel has operated in Malaysia for more than five decades, with the country serving as one of its assembly, test and manufacturing locations. The Penang expansion adds advanced packaging to those existing capabilities.

“The new Penang facility represents the next phase of that journey,” Lee said. “It expands our capabilities across advanced packaging, assembly, test, research and design.”

According to Lee, the facility will support end-to-end advanced packaging manufacturing. Wafers produced at multiple fabrication plants will be brought into the facility before finished products are shipped out.

The expansion will also allow Intel Malaysia to handle more advanced products and technically complex manufacturing workloads alongside its existing operations.

“It positions Intel Malaysia to support more advanced products and increasingly sophisticated manufacturing workloads,” Lee said.

Malaysia has spent decades building its semiconductor manufacturing base around areas including assembly and testing. The country is also seeking to develop more capabilities in areas such as advanced packaging and chip design.

Lee said the country already has manufacturing experience and an established semiconductor ecosystem, but further development is needed in engineering and research capabilities.

“The next step is building deeper capabilities in talent, research and innovation, particularly in advanced packaging, design enablement, automation, materials science and manufacturing analytics,” Lee said.

### Semiconductor talent requirements are changing

The skills required by Intel’s manufacturing operations are also changing as semiconductor production incorporates more automation, data analysis and advanced engineering.

Lee said Intel increasingly requires workers who can combine semiconductor knowledge with expertise from other technical disciplines.

Key areas include integrated circuit design and validation, advanced packaging process development, systems engineering, test engineering and reliability. Intel is also seeking capabilities in data analytics, machine learning, AI software, cybersecurity, robotics and manufacturing automation.

“The hardest skills to find are often at the intersections — engineers who can connect semiconductor domain knowledge with data science, statistics and AI to improve areas such as yield analysis, predictive maintenance and supply-chain optimisation,” Lee said.

Addressing those gaps requires greater exposure to areas including semiconductor device physics, design for manufacturability, packaging, testing and validation, according to Lee.

Intel works with Malaysian universities including Universiti Sains Malaysia and Universiti Malaysia Perlis on areas such as advanced packaging research and curriculum development. The company has also expanded partnerships with Tunku Abdul Rahman University of Management and Technology and Multimedia University around AI skills.

“Courses, internships, cooperative education programmes and joint laboratories can give students earlier exposure to real tools, datasets and workflows,” Lee said.

### Malaysia’s place in a diversified supply chain

Intel’s manufacturing network also operates against a backdrop of export controls, geopolitical tensions and semiconductor companies diversifying production across multiple locations.

Lee said semiconductor supply-chain resilience requires companies to balance efficiency with stability and flexibility across their manufacturing networks.

“A resilient semiconductor supply chain balances efficiency with stability and flexibility,” Lee said. “It is geographically diversified, transparent and able to respond quickly to changing conditions.”

He said trust within the semiconductor supply chain depends on consistent quality, security, traceability and manufacturing integrity throughout the product lifecycle.

Lee said Malaysia’s established semiconductor ecosystem, workforce and integration into global supply chains give the country a role within a geographically diversified manufacturing network.

Looking ahead, Lee said Intel Malaysia’s progress should be assessed by the capabilities and responsibilities it develops within the company’s global operations rather than investment or employment figures alone.

“I would like to see Malaysia recognised as a centre of excellence for advanced packaging, manufacturing innovation, automation and engineering leadership,” Lee said. “That means developing world-class talent, deploying next-generation manufacturing technologies and taking on increasingly critical global responsibilities.”

Lee also pointed to collaboration with universities, suppliers, startups and other industry participants as part of that development.

“If Malaysia becomes a place where advanced technologies are developed, industrialised and scaled for the world, that would mark a successful next chapter not only for Intel Malaysia, but for Malaysia’s role in the global semiconductor ecosystem,” Lee said.

stories.title: Data centres face rising cyber threats, regulatory lag
stories.summary: Data centre operators globally, including in India, face increasing cyber threats and operational vulnerabilities, necessitating proactive measures beyond current regulations. A lithium battery fire in Delhi disrupted Google Cloud across three Indian metros, highlighting operational resilience challenges.
stories.content:
Data centre operators cannot afford to wait for regulation before strengthening cyber resilience, redundancy, and remote access controls, according to Nick Haan, Field CTO at Claroty. Two years after UK data centres were recognised as critical national infrastructure, minimum cybersecurity requirements are still absent, even as infrastructure becomes more vital and a tempting target for cyber threat actors.Not every threat is an accident; data centres are inherently vulnerable due to complex digital and physical systems, high energy demands, and minimal tolerance for downtime. Earlier this year, Russian hacktivist group Killnet breached a French data centre and its backup power supplier, claiming access to 120,000 UPS units and exfiltrating data. Furthermore, a fire at a data centre in Almere, Netherlands, in May disrupted Utrecht University, the Chamber of Commerce, and IBM Cloud. A month later, a lithium battery fire in Delhi triggered an emergency shutdown that knocked out Google Cloud across three Indian metros for a prolonged period.

Despite high physical security, threat actors often target data centres through the cyber layer. Claroty's research across over 174,000 data centre infrastructure devices found that while only 0.4 per cent were directly internet-exposed, 18 per cent were just one hop away, with power distribution units (PDUs) posing the highest risk at 41 per cent. Remote access remains a significant challenge, often managed through ad hoc, disparate systems that create visibility and control gaps. The infrastructure, including DNS servers and domain controllers, requires rigorous security from the outset, not as an afterthought. Third-party contractors further complicate managing potential access points.Operators do not need to wait for new legislation; existing guidance like ISO 27002 and FIPS provides established approaches for individual accounts, logging, and access control, moving beyond shared credentials. The key to real resilience involves interrogating redundancy rather than assuming its effectiveness, ensuring independent systems prevent single points of failure. Claroty's Team82 researchers discovered critical vulnerabilities in Vertiv's widely used Liebert UPS network cards, which could allow an attacker to bypass authentication and remotely issue an "output OFF" command, shutting down protected devices. Data centre operators should assess their cyber-physical systems for blind spots and vulnerabilities, particularly concerning remote access and power distribution units. They must also interrogate their redundancy strategies to ensure independent systems and prevent single points of failure, including for backup power and security measures. stories.title: AI's data centre overhaul forcing a network rethink
stories.summary: AI training workloads are exposing network bottlenecks that leave expensive GPUs idle between compute steps, driving operators to redesign facilities around lossless Ethernet fabrics. Traditional data centre network architectures built for general-purpose traffic are proving inadequate for GPU-cluster communication.
stories.why_it_matters: Networks are now a first-order design constraint, shifting capex toward high-performance switching and specialised fabrics. Vendors of conventional networking gear face displacement, while AI-optimised fabric providers capture a growing share of build budgets.
stories.content:
Thu, 24th Sep 2026 (Yesterday)
Data centres are at a structural turning point as artificial intelligence reshapes not just compute demand, but the very assumptions underpinning networking and infrastructure design.

What was once an incremental evolution of cloud architecture is now a wholesale redesign of how data moves and how systems scale. At the centre of this shift is a simple but increasingly unforgiving reality: AI workloads do not behave like traditional cloud applications.

Rather, they are continuous, tightly synchronised, and massively parallel. Instead of isolated requests and responses, modern AI training involves thousands of GPUs exchanging data simultaneously, often across racks and even across facilities.

The result is a network environment where performance is no longer a background concern, but has a direct impact on business performance.

The industry has already lived through two major networking eras. The "north-south" model of early cloud computing was built around user traffic entering and exiting data centres, with relatively modest internal communication needs.

That evolved into an "east-west" world driven by microservices, where server-to-server traffic inside the data centre became dominant. Now AI has pushed this pattern into overdrive. Internal traffic is no longer just frequent but also constant and highly sensitive to delay. In effect, east-west traffic has become the entire workload.

### 'Pushing the piano'

The analogy often used inside the industry is that of "pushing pianos around the office." Instead of individual tasks moving independently, thousands of components must co-ordinate large, heavy data movements in lockstep. If one participant falters, the entire group slows.

Even small inefficiencies can cascade into queue buildup, GPU idle time, and significantly higher training costs. With accelerator clusters costing millions of dollars and operating continuously, every second of inefficiency becomes directly measurable in financial terms.

This is driving a rapid shift in architectural requirements. Oversubscription ratios that were once comfortably designed at 3:1 or 5:1 are now collapsing toward 1:1 models in AI clusters, where every GPU must communicate with every other GPU simultaneously.

Bandwidth demands are rising just as sharply, with 400Gbps Ethernet becoming baseline, 800Gbps deployments accelerating, and 1.6Tbps already on the horizon. Traditional "best effort" networking is increasingly viewed as insufficient for workloads that require predictable, near-lossless performance.

### An evolving technology mix

To meet these demands, data centre operators are adopting technologies such as RDMA over Converged Ethernet (RoCE), along with congestion management mechanisms like Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) and Priority Flow Control (PFC). These tools are designed to minimise buffering and prevent packet drops in environments where even microsecond-level delays can propagate into system-wide slowdowns.

At a higher level, the balance of compute itself is shifting. The GPU is becoming the primary unit of computation, while the CPU increasingly plays a co-ordinating role. This inversion is reshaping how servers are designed and how networking stacks are integrated.

Technologies such as SmartNICs and data processing units are offloading networking, security, and telemetry tasks closer to the fabric, reducing CPU overhead and improving synchronisation across distributed workloads.

These architectural changes are also driving physical transformation. Power densities of 50 to 150 kilowatts per rack are pushing air cooling beyond its limits, accelerating the adoption of direct-to-chip liquid cooling and immersion systems.

Networking hardware is undergoing a similar transition. Electrical interconnects are reaching their practical limits, accelerating a shift toward optical technologies. Co-packaged optics, which bring photonic interfaces closer to compute units, are reducing both latency and energy consumption, while enabling higher bandwidth density within constrained physical footprints.

### The changing role of the network

In this emerging environment, the network is no longer passive but is becoming an active participant in workload management. Model updates, fine-tuned weights, and inference optimisation data are now treated as first-class traffic types, alongside traditional application data.

And the network is not just a neutral transporter of data. Production-grade AI data centres need to run on a lossless, high-performance network fabric – supporting low latency, preventing oversubscription, and able to deliver east-west bandwidth at scale. Organisations aren't looking for a data centre network, they need an AI fabric, where the network is part of the application itself.

Taken together, these shifts point to three structural changes that define the AI infrastructure era. First, the network now sits directly in the critical path of compute performance and financial efficiency.

Second, networking systems are becoming adaptive, continuously optimising in response to workload behaviour rather than static configuration.

Third, compute and networking design are converging, with hardware and software increasingly co-designed rather than independently optimised.

The implication is that future competitiveness will not be determined solely by faster processors or larger clusters, but by how effectively compute and networking are integrated into a unified architecture.

Data centres are evolving into tightly coupled, GPU-dominated systems supported by lossless, high-bandwidth optical fabrics, while the edge becomes a distributed extension of the same intelligence layer.

The trajectory is clear: infrastructure is shifting from general-purpose computing environments into highly specialised AI factories. What once looked like incremental upgrades in speed and capacity is now a fundamental redesign of the digital economy's physical backbone.

stories.title: AEMC opens consultation on data centre network cost recovery
stories.summary: The Australian Energy Market Commission has opened consultation on two rule change requests from Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen that would have data centres and other large loads pay more directly for the network costs they trigger. The proposals target connection-driven upgrades that are currently socialised across all consumers.
stories.why_it_matters: Cost-reflective charging would add a material new expense line for large data centre projects and could reshape site selection toward locations with spare grid capacity. It also answers political pressure over whether AI infrastructure should be subsidised by household power bills.
stories.content:
The Australian Energy Market Commission (AEMC) **has opened consultation on two rule change requests** aimed at making data centres and other large electricity loads contribute more directly to the network costs they cause or accelerate. The requests were submitted by Federal Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen in July and seek changes to the National Electricity Rules (NER) covering both distribution and transmission connections.

The AEMC said the consultation comes as the scale and speed of data centre growth is testing existing cost-recovery arrangements. The Commission’s consultation paper says the Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO) forecasts data centre electricity consumption could rise from about 5 TWh in 2025-26 to around 15 TWh by 2029-30, equivalent to about 8 percent of National Electricity Market (NEM) operational consumption. By 2044-45, the forecast reaches about 41 TWh, or 13.5 percent.

The AEMC said connecting parties already pay for infrastructure required to facilitate their connections, as well as ongoing charges for use of the shared network. The issue under consultation is whether those arrangements adequately capture the costs and risks associated with the scale of some future large-load connections.

Bowen’s requests identify seven potential gaps in the current framework, and the AEMC is seeking views on whether they exist and how material they are.

These include the possibility that a large load connecting to a distribution network could trigger upstream transmission augmentation costs that are partly recovered from other customers; the risk of network assets being built for projects that subsequently do not proceed or use less capacity than expected; and uncertainty over the treatment of clustered large loads requiring major shared network investment.

### Large loads

The AEMC is also asking whether there is insufficient public information about existing and prospective large loads to support effective forecasting and network planning, whether transmission-connected large loads should contribute to jurisdictional scheme costs, and whether the rules provide enough guidance around pricing for transmission connection services.

On jurisdictional schemes, the AEMC notes that the existing NER provides a mechanism for recovering such costs from distribution-connected customers, but no equivalent framework currently exists for transmission-connected customers.

Among the changes Bowen proposes is a requirement for network service providers to apply prudential requirements to large connections, alongside limits on their ability to recover stranded customer-specific assets from the broader consumer base.

The proposals would also require network service providers to provide information on existing and prospective large loads to AEMO for a proposed public large-load register. Other measures would make it easier for connection applicants to voluntarily fund, or bring forward, major network augmentations and introduce greater consistency in transmission connection pricing through an Australian Energy Regulator (AER) guideline.

### Cost-recovery

The cost-recovery consultation is one part of a broader AEMC data centre reform program. The Commission’s earlier advice to Energy Ministers recommended measures covering clean energy procurement, firming capacity, market registration and demand flexibility. AEMO has separately proposed reforms to improve the operational visibility of large inverter-based loads, while further rule changes are expected covering data centre contracting obligations and the connection process.

The AEMC said it will consider the interlinkages across these reforms, and its consultation paper notes that connection pricing can depend on the registration status of a connection applicant, creating an interaction between the cost-recovery proposals and the operational-visibility reforms.

The Commission is also coordinating its work with other regulatory processes. These include a forthcoming AER review of distribution connection-charge guidelines, NSW proposals for network cost allocation, and the Federal government’s emerging national standards for new data centres. The AEMC notes that most elements of the NSW proposals are very similar to the solutions proposed in the rule change requests.

The AEMC expects to publish a draft determination on the two rule changes on 1 April 2027. The Commission says the timetable has been extended because of the complexity of the proposals and their interaction with its wider data centre reform program. Submissions close on 5 November 2026.

stories.title: Schneider Electric launches hybrid data centre cooler
stories.summary: Data centre operators can now mix air and liquid cooling in one unit as AI workloads push rack densities higher across facilities.
stories.content:
Thu, 24th Sep 2026 (Yesterday)
Schneider Electric has launched a new coolant distribution unit for data centres that combines liquid and air cooling in a single system.

Called the WCDU, the product is aimed at high-density AI deployments and is designed to work with fan wall air-cooling systems as well as standalone liquid cooling setups.

The launch adds a larger system to Schneider Electric's Motivair cooling range as operators look for ways to support denser computing equipment without committing too early to one cooling architecture. The unit is intended to let data centre operators shift the balance between air and liquid cooling as workload plans evolve, rather than redesigning a hall from the ground up.

That reflects a wider market shift as AI infrastructure drives higher rack densities and pushes operators towards liquid cooling. At the same time, many facilities still rely on air cooling in at least part of the hall, creating demand for systems that bridge both approaches.

### Corridor design

The WCDU was developed for technical corridor deployments, where cooling distribution equipment is installed outside the white space used for IT hardware. Schneider Electric says this arrangement can ease maintenance and free up space inside the data hall.

The unit uses top-entry connections and is designed with zero lateral clearance, which can simplify installation in space-constrained sites. It also places pumps, heat exchangers and other CDU components within a single steel frame.

In practice, the WCDU can be integrated with existing fan wall environments or deployed as a standalone unit. That gives operators a retrofit option if they already use fan walls and want to add more liquid cooling to support denser systems.

A single WCDU can provide cooling capacity of up to 3.5MW at 1.5 litres per minute per kW, and 2.5MW at 2.0 litres per minute per kW. Up to 20 units can be linked in group mode, making the system suitable for data halls in the 30MW to 40MW range, according to Schneider Electric.

### Efficiency focus

The unit supports approach temperatures as low as 2°C and can operate with warmer facility water system temperatures. In data centre cooling systems, lower approach temperatures can improve overall efficiency by narrowing the gap between facility water temperature and the temperature required at the cooling interface.

Schneider Electric says this can improve power usage effectiveness and reduce operating costs across the broader cooling system. The WCDU also includes hot-swappable pumps, pressure-independent control valves, 25-micron filters and a 15-inch touchscreen human-machine interface.

For sites that need additional backup, configurations up to 2.5MW can be specified with N+1 redundancy. That provides pump and valve backup intended to keep cooling available during maintenance or an unexpected component failure.

The addition broadens Schneider Electric's liquid cooling portfolio, which now spans CDU systems from 105kW to 3.5MW. The company positions the range as covering row-based, corridor-based and other deployment models.

Andrew Bradner, Senior Vice President of the Cooling Business at Schneider Electric, said the product is designed to support changing data centre layouts.

"As the only CDU that brings together both liquid and air cooling within a single solution, we're delivering a level of flexibility the market hasn't seen before," said Andrew Bradner, Senior Vice President of the Cooling Business at Schneider Electric. "This approach allows operators to deploy more efficiently, support a wider range of liquid cooling infrastructure configurations, and significantly reduce time to deployment."

stories.title: SUBCO eyes 2029 completion for three new Indo-Pacific cable systems
stories.summary: SUBCO says it will complete three new submarine cable systems totalling 40,000 km by 2029, linking Australia to Asia and the US. APX North will run 9,500 km from Sydney to Japan via Guam, complemented by APX East-2 and a third system across the Indo-Pacific.
stories.why_it_matters: The new systems add badly needed redundancy and capacity on Australia-Asia routes, where a small number of outages have repeatedly disrupted connectivity. They also strengthen Australia's position as a connectivity hub rather than a bandwidth outlier.
stories.content:
SUBCO, a developer, owner, and operator of next-generation submarine fiber-optic cable infrastructure, has announced that it will be building three new subsea cables connecting Australia to several locations in Asia and the US over 40,000 km.

According to a press release, APX North will span 9,500 km, connecting Sydney to Japan via Guam. APX East-2 will be 10,000 km long and connect Guam to Los Angeles. APX West is a 4,600 km cable connecting Perth to Singapore with branches to Jakarta and Batam. Each cable will contain 24 fiber pairs, with SUBCO targeting completion of all three systems by 2029.

“People have been slow to understand that AI factories are dead without massive subsea connectivity to carry tokens from factory to customers. Hundreds and hundreds of terabits per second. That’s why we are about to undertake the single largest subsea infrastructure build ever by a carrier in the Indo-Pacific. Not only is the build itself huge, but the timeframe is compressed with over 40,000km of cable to be installed in just over three years. Our team has signed up for the challenge, and will grow significantly as each system reaches CIF,” said Bevan Slattery, SUBCO Founder and Co-Chief Executive Officer.

The co-CEO noted that APX Eat-2, connecting Guam and Los Angeles, is vital for trans-Pacific digital traffic and expects the system to be incredibly popular. Similarly, APEX West is important for resiliency and interconnection at hubs in Batam and Jakarta.

“Singapore and Indonesia remain critical to Asia’s connectivity landscape, and their strategic importance will only grow as bandwidth demand accelerates, and new interconnection hubs are needed to deliver greater flexibility and route diversity. We are building as much of that as possible into our system design and making that available to our cornerstone customers through APX West,” said Slattery.

The company announced in June that its SMAP cable system connecting Sydney, Melbourne, Adelaide, and Perth was ready for service. The 5,000 km cable features 16 fiber pairs and delivers more than 400 Tbps of capacity.

stories.title: Thai bill proposes data center licensing, environmental & health impact assessments
stories.summary: A Thai MP has tabled a draft bill that would introduce mandatory licensing for data centres plus environmental and community health impact assessments for all projects. Operators would need approval from the Ministry of Digital Economy and Society before building or expanding.
stories.why_it_matters: If enacted, Thailand would move from one of Southeast Asia's most permissive regimes to a structured approvals process, adding time and uncertainty to project timelines. Established operators with compliant facilities gain an advantage over new entrants rushing to market.
stories.content:
A Thai member of Parliament has recently introduced a draft bill proposing sweeping changes to its data center rules, including requiring licensing, and environmental and community health impact assessments on all data center projects, according to local reports. If passed, operators would need to obtain a licence from the Ministry of Digital Economy and Society, locate their facilities in areas zoned for factories, must be a Thai-registered company, and provide a guarantee when applying for a licence.

The proposals, which were introduced by MP Supachai Jaisamut, seek to regulate digital infrastructure pertaining to project locations, environmental and health impact assessments, electricity and water supplies, and data sovereignty, with key numerical thresholds to be specified later in secondary legislation.

The public including operators, users of services and affected communities are invited to contribute their views thru to 15 October.

With the aim of protecting Thai resources, the draft bill requires high usage data centers to either generate their own electricity, buy directly from licensed private power producers, or a combination of both.

Similarly, data centers with high water consumption must have sufficient water from their own sources, without using public sources. They must also keep heat released and noise pollution within limits to be prescribed by the minister.

The draft requires operators that collect, store, process or hold in custody Thai nationals’ personal data, data of Thai-registered entities, or information of government departments, public organisations and other state agencies, to store those data in Thailand, with strict conditions for any transfers outside of the country.

Operators must also ensure Thai nationals make up at least half of all personnel performing system supervision duties, as well as use minimum prescribed local content for their materials and equipment.

The penalty for operating without a licence is imprisonment for up to five years, a fine of at least THB10 million, or both, as well as an additional fine of up to THB1 million a day as long as a licence is not obtained. An operator which fails to store Thai nationals’ personal data in Thailand could face up to three years’ imprisonment, a fine of at least THB6 million, or both.

Existing operators have up to 180 days from the date the law comes into force (ministerial licensing regulations) to apply for a licence.

stories.title: Australian data centre operators raise AU$35bn in 2026 as debt funding surges
stories.summary: A Reserve Bank of Australia staff analysis shows Australian data centre operators have raised at least AU$35 billion so far in 2026, with debt making up 85 percent of new capital. The sector now accounts for 16 percent of all funding raised by Australian non-financial corporations, a striking share for a single industry.
stories.why_it_matters: The scale of debt-funded expansion signals both confidence in AI-driven demand and growing systemic exposure: heavy leverage could amplify sector stress if capacity outruns tenant commitments. Policymakers are watching this boom as much as investors are.
stories.content:
Australian data centre operators have raised at least AU$35bn in funding so far in 2026, with debt accounting for 85 percent of new capital, according to a Reserve Bank of Australia staff analysis. The RBA’s **Data Centre Financing in Australia** found that data centre operators accounted for 16 percent of funding raised by Australian non-financial corporations across the markets covered by its research.

The figure represents a significant increase from the AU$24bn raised in 2025 and an annual average of AU$4.6bn between 2020 and 2024.

The analysis, by RBA economist Bradley Speed, covers Australian-domiciled companies operating data centres in Australia. Its sample includes NextDC, CDC, Firmus, Goodman, Macquarie Technology, AirTrunk and local funding vehicles associated with Stack Infrastructure and Equinix. The RBA said its estimates should be treated as a lower bound because coverage of private transactions is incomplete and the data does not capture some single-bank lending.

### Debt dominates data centre funding

Debt accounted for 85 percent of new funding raised by Australian data centre operators in 2026, with syndicated lending providing the largest share. Operators raised approximately AU$25bn through syndicated loans, which accounted for around three-quarters of data centre financing in 2025 and 2026 to date.

Data centre operators also accounted for 17 percent of new syndicated lending during 2026, up from 6 percent in 2025. A further AU$13bn in syndicated lending deals had been announced during the year but had not yet been completed.

The RBA said syndicated lending was attractive because it enabled operators to secure larger loans through pooled lender exposure, while generally being more accessible than corporate bond markets for companies without investment-grade credit ratings.

Approximately 70 percent of syndicated lending raised by Australian data centre operators was denominated in Australian dollars, with most of the remainder in US dollars.

The sector accounted for 7 percent of new Australian-dollar syndicated borrowing in 2026 to date. The RBA also found that loan pricing was broadly comparable with that of other non-financial corporations. The median spread on syndicated loans to data centre operators since 2024 was 185 basis points, compared with 175 basis points for other non-financial corporations.

It suggested that tenant pre-commitments could be helping to mitigate risks associated with rapid expansion. “Data centres’ higher use of syndicated lending is consistent with the rest of the Australian non-financial corporate sector,” the report said.

### Bonds and equity remain secondary

Corporate bonds accounted for AU$5bn, or 14 percent, of data centre funding in 2026 to date, up from 4 percent in 2025. The RBA said bond issuance remained relatively limited, potentially reflecting the costs associated with mandatory disclosures and credit ratings.

However, it noted that bonds could become more attractive as operators grow and seek more diversified funding sources, particularly because they do not carry financial maintenance covenants.

Data centre operators raised a further AU$1.5bn through public equity issuance in 2026, while private equity funding reached approximately AU$4bn. Private equity activity had been concentrated largely in Firmus, which conducted three private equity issuances during the year. The RBA however cautioned that its visibility of private transactions was imperfect and that some funding could be missing from the estimates.

### Limited evidence of crowding out

Despite the rapid growth in funding, the RBA said data centre financing remained relatively small compared with the size of Australian capital markets. It found little evidence that the sector had materially affected financing conditions for other borrowers.

The analysis also found no evidence that access to finance was currently limiting data centre investment in Australia. The RBA said this could change as operators’ funding requirements increased, but expected the sector to make greater use of a wider range of domestic and offshore funding sources as it expanded.

The RBA added that local operators had made slightly larger contributions to investment in Australia’s data centre sector than foreign firms to date. It also identified the capital raised by local operators as a potentially useful leading indicator of future investment, given that these companies tend to rely on external funding to support construction.

The author added the caveat that the findings didn’t necessarily represent the view of the bank, adding that the analysis also excluded funding raised by overseas companies where the connection to specific Australian data centre investment was unclear.
